nameStory: This massive jellyfish gets its majestic name from its flowing, golden-brown tentacles that cascade from its bell like a lion's magnificent mane. When the tentacles stream behind the jelly as it moves through the water, the resemblance to a big cat's flowing hair is unmistakable.
description: The Lion's Mane Jelly is one of the ocean's true giants and the largest known jellyfish species in the world. Picture a dinner plate-sized (or much larger!) reddish-brown umbrella floating through the water, trailing what looks like silky ribbons behind it. These incredible creatures can grow enormous - the largest ever recorded had a bell 7 feet across with tentacles stretching 120 feet long. In New England waters, they're typically smaller but still impressively sized, often reaching several feet across.

idTips.label: Flowing tentacle clusters
idTips.description: Hundreds of thin, hair-like tentacles hang in distinct clusters from the bell's edge, streaming like golden or reddish-brown silk ribbons through the water

idTips.label: Large, dome-shaped bell
idTips.description: The bell resembles a flattened dome or shallow bowl, often translucent with a reddish-brown, orange, or yellowish tint that becomes more vibrant toward the center

idTips.label: Radial pattern on bell
idTips.description: Look for spoke-like lines radiating from the center of the bell outward, creating a wagon wheel pattern that's visible through the translucent flesh

idTips.label: Impressive size
idTips.description: In New England waters, bells typically range from dinner plate to trash can lid size, making them noticeably larger than most other jellies you'll encounter

idTips.label: Graceful swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with slow, rhythmic pulsing of the bell, with tentacles trailing elegantly behind like a living underwater parachute

habitat: Lion's Mane Jellies prefer the cold waters of New England's coast, especially in the Gulf of Maine and Massachusetts Bay. You're most likely to spot them from boats, docks, or beaches in deeper coastal waters, though they sometimes drift into harbors and bays. They thrive in the chilly, nutrient-rich waters where the Labrador Current meets warmer southern waters.

seasonality.spring: Large adults begin appearing in New England waters as they follow cold currents southward. This is when you might see the biggest specimens of the year.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for sightings, especially in July and August when they're most commonly encountered near the surface. Warmer water brings them closer to shore.
seasonality.fall: Still visible but becoming less common as water temperatures begin to drop. Late fall sightings are usually of smaller individuals.
seasonality.winter: Rarely seen in New England waters during the coldest months, as they retreat to deeper waters or follow currents further offshore.

funFact: The largest Lion's Mane Jelly ever recorded was found right here in Massachusetts waters in 1865 - its tentacles were longer than a blue whale and could have stretched across an entire football field with room to spare!
confusionNotes: Most other New England jellies are much smaller and lack the distinctive flowing tentacle clusters. Moon jellies have four obvious horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs visible through their bell and much shorter tentacles around the edge, while Lion's Manes have long streaming tentacles in distinct bunches.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fearsome appearance, Lion's Mane Jellies in New England waters deliver a relatively mild sting compared to tropical species - more like a nettle sting than anything dangerous. However, even dead jellies washed up on beaches can still sting, so admire from a distance.
compareHints: The Lion's Mane Jelly is much larger than its relatives, the Atlantic Lion's Mane Jelly and Dwarf Lion's Mane Jelly. While all three share the characteristic flowing tentacles, the true Lion's Mane reaches gigantic proportions that dwarf its cousins. The Atlantic Lion's Mane tends to be more consistently reddish, while the Dwarf species rarely exceeds the size of a dinner plate.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Within the Lion's Mane family, the Atlantic species sits right in the middle size-wise - bigger than the tiny Dwarf Lion's Mane but much smaller than the Giant Lion's Mane that can grow huge in colder northern waters.
The dwarf lion's mane is significantly smaller than the giant lion's mane jelly (Cyanea capillata), which can have bells several feet across.
